slides.title: A thousand marks need not mean a thousand shapes
keyPoints: Many placements may reuse one style
Position changes independently of style
Measure repeated payload before changing ownership
slides.narration: A drawing tool places marks at different horizontal positions. A mark has a style name and size as well as its position. Storing all three values in every mark is easy to understand, and for a small drawing it may be the best design. Now imagine each style also includes a large shape outline. Copying that outline into ten thousand marks spends memory on the same information again and again. Our question is whether we can keep that common part once without making the positions common too. Before designing the sharing, measure the repeated data. The small strings in this teaching example do not by themselves prove a memory saving.
actions: Ask learners to separate facts about a shape from facts about one placement.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch11.json → Repeated data can outweigh useful differences

question.prompt: Which field must stay local when two marks share one style?
question.answer: The position belongs to each individual mark; sharing it would couple independent placements.

slides.title: The direct value model is a valid starting point
keyPoints: Each mark owns its own name, size, and position
Changing one value does not change another
Repeated payload grows with the number of marks
slides.narration: Run this complete value-based model before introducing pointers. Each Mark owns a string, a size, and a position. The brace lists supply those fields in declaration order. A const reference in draw borrows one mark so printing does not copy its string. We first draw two equal styles at different positions, then change only the left style's size. The right mark remains size twelve because it owns a separate value. That independence is a useful default, not a defect. The cost appears only if the style payload becomes large and many marks repeat it. Any sharing design must preserve the independence of position while deliberately changing how the style is stored.
actions: Predict the last two output lines before running.

question.prompt: Why does changing left.size not change right.size?
question.answer: They are two independent int members in two different Mark objects.

slides.title: A pool can share the wrong thing perfectly
keyPoints: The lookup key defines interchangeability
Name alone loses the requested size
Well-typed code can preserve the wrong identity
slides.narration: This demonstration intentionally uses an incomplete lookup key. The bad pool remembers styles by name only. Requesting stamp size twelve creates an object; requesting stamp size twenty finds the same name and returns the earlier object. The output therefore reports requested twenty but received twelve. Nothing crashed, no object died early, and the pointer is valid. The failure is a false claim about equality: the key treats two different styles as interchangeable. The correct chapter pool uses both name and size. If color later becomes shared state, color must enter the key too. A compiler cannot infer that design promise from the name of a map.
actions: Ask which one field must be added to the key before discussing pointer changes.

question.prompt: Would replacing shared_ptr with another owner repair the wrong size?
question.answer: No. The lookup identity is incomplete; the key must include every field that affects the shared style.

slides.title: Share the stable facts; keep each use separate
keyPoints: Intrinsic state: shared name and size
Extrinsic state: the individual x position
A Mark owns a handle, not another full style
slides.narration: Flyweight is a design that shares repeated state while leaving each use's changing details outside the shared object. The shared part has the technical name intrinsic state. In our chapter that is the style name and size. The per-use part is extrinsic state, here the horizontal position. These names describe a design choice, not a property that every program must assign the same way. A StylePool returns owners of an immutable Style, and a Mark stores one such owner beside its own position. Two marks can refer to the same style without becoming the same mark. That separation is the central mechanism to find in code.
actions: Ask learners to describe a third mark that shares style but differs in position.

question.prompt: If x were stored in shared Style, what visible bug could moving one mark cause?
question.answer: Every mark sharing that Style would observe the changed x, so independent placements would become coupled.

slides.title: The contract we must preserve
keyPoints: Share styles only when both name and size match.
Keep each mark position separate.
Reject empty names, size outside 1–100, and missing style pointers.
slides.narration:
Several marks, one immutable style. A map interns immutable Style objects by a complete structured key. shared_ptr allows marks to retain styles after a pool is destroyed.

Share styles only when both name and size match. Keep each mark position separate. Reject empty names, size outside 1–100, and missing style pointers.

One active pool returns the same object for the same key. Published Style objects are immutable. Each Mark owns its own position and shares only intrinsic style state. These are the rules that define a correct extension, even if it has the right C++ types. Store style fields by value for a small number of small styles. Integer style IDs into a stable central table can use less per-mark memory but require a clear table lifetime and ID-validity contract.

question.prompt: Which promise would a new Flyweight implementation be allowed to break?
question.answer: None of the stated requirements. The implementation may change, but these rules remain: One active pool returns the same object for the same key. Published Style objects are immutable. Each Mark owns its own position and shares only intrinsic style state.

slides.title: Repeated data can outweigh useful differences
keyPoints: A drawing tool places many marks on a page.
The limitation appears when the shared portion becomes large.
slides.narration:
A drawing tool places many marks on a page. A mark has a style name, a style size, and a horizontal position. Thousands of marks may use the same style while each position differs. For a few marks, store all three fields directly in every object. That is simple, clear, and often the right answer.

The limitation appears when the shared portion becomes large. Imagine that a style later contains a loaded shape outline or a rendering table. Copying that payload for every mark may consume far more memory than the positions themselves. Before changing the design, measure the repeated data and the number of uses. Our small program keeps style data intentionally short so the ownership mechanism is visible; it is not evidence that this tiny representation saves memory.

question.prompt: Two marks share a name and font size but appear at different positions. Which data can they share?

slides.title: Split stable shared data from each use
keyPoints: Flyweight is a memory-sharing design that stores repeated state once and gives each use a connection to it.
StylePool looks up a style by a Key containing both name and size.
The key is a std::pair<std::string, int>, not two fields joined into an unstructured string.
slides.narration:
Flyweight is a memory-sharing design that stores repeated state once and gives each use a connection to it. The shared state is called intrinsic state. Here name and size identify the style. The state that belongs to a particular use is called extrinsic state. Here x is the mark's position. A Mark holds a shared style owner and its own x value. Two Marks can therefore agree on style without becoming the same mark.

StylePool looks up a style by a Key containing both name and size. If that key already exists, it returns another shared owner of the same Style object. Otherwise it creates one immutable Style, stores an owner in the map, and returns another owner. Reusing an existing object is often called interning. It is useful only when equality of the chosen key truly means the shared data is interchangeable.

The key is a std::pair<std::string, int>, not two fields joined into an unstructured string. A pair keeps field boundaries unambiguous. If a later style includes color, color must become part of the key too. A pool keyed only by name would wrongly reuse dot size twelve for a request for dot size twenty. The visible mistake would be a correct position with the wrong style size.

slides.title: Read the shared pointer type carefully
keyPoints: StylePtr is an alias for std::shared_ptr<const Style>.
The pool constructs the object with make_shared<const Style>.
A shared_ptr copy increments a shared ownership count; it does not copy the Style.
slides.narration:
StylePtr is an alias for std::shared_ptr<const Style>. shared_ptr means several owners can keep the same object alive. const Style means the object reached through this owner is read-only. It is not the same as const shared_ptr<Style>, which would prevent reseating that particular pointer variable but would still permit changing the Style through it.

The pool constructs the object with make_shared<const Style>. The actual allocated Style is const, not merely viewed through one const handle while another mutable handle is retained. Its fields are initialized once and then read. Immutability means the object does not change after construction. That matters because a mutation to one shared style could otherwise change every mark using it. The public fields remain safe to read because access is through a pointer to const; the pool gives out no mutable owner.

A shared_ptr copy increments a shared ownership count; it does not copy the Style. When one pointer is destroyed, the count decreases. The object remains alive while at least one owner remains. The pool owns styles through its map, and each Mark owns its style through style_. This is shared ownership, so an ownership diagram must not imply that a mark exclusively owns its style. The arrows are labeled shared owner to make that distinction explicit.

slides.title: Trace a lookup and a draw
keyPoints: main requests (dot,12) twice.
Mark left takes an owner of the twelve-size style and stores x = 3.
In draw, const auto& name borrows the string inside Style while the Mark's owner keeps the Style alive.
slides.narration:
main requests (dot,12) twice. The first lookup misses, creates one Style, and stores it. The second lookup finds the existing entry and returns found->second, which is the map's shared_ptr value. first and same therefore point to the same object. A request for (dot,20) uses a different key and receives a different object. The pointer equality checks test identity, not merely equal field values.

Mark left takes an owner of the twelve-size style and stores x = 3. Mark right receives another owner of that same style and stores x = 8. draw reads the shared name and size, then appends its own position. The outputs dot/12@3 and dot/12@8 show the separation directly. Neither draw call changes the style or the other mark.

In draw, const auto& name borrows the string inside Style while the Mark's owner keeps the Style alive. const auto size copies the small integer. Both are suitable choices: copying an int is cheap; copying the string is unnecessary for this local read. The returned formatted string is a new owned value. It does not expose a reference into shared state and remains valid after the Mark is destroyed. Mark explicitly defaults its copy operations, which suppresses automatic generation of move operations. Constructing from std::move(left) therefore copies the shared owner; both marks stay usable. This value-like policy avoids a moved-from Mark with a null style.

slides.title: Lifetime is independent of the pool scope
keyPoints: The program creates a short-lived StylePool inside a nested scope and saves one returned owner in survivor outside that scope.
The pool uses strong owners, so it also retains each style until the pool is destroyed or entries are removed.
The compiler checks const access and pointer types; it cannot prove that the key includes every meaningful field.
slides.narration:
The program creates a short-lived StylePool inside a nested scope and saves one returned owner in survivor outside that scope. When the pool is destroyed, its map releases its owner. survivor still owns the Style, so reading survivor->name afterward is valid. This test checks a real advantage of shared ownership: the pool's lifetime need not enclose every use.

The pool uses strong owners, so it also retains each style until the pool is destroyed or entries are removed. An unused style does not vanish merely because its last Mark disappears. That is a cache-retention policy, not a leak caused by missing delete. A long-running application may require a size limit, explicit clearing, or weak_ptr entries. A weak pointer observes a shared object without keeping it alive, but it requires checking whether the object still exists before reuse. That complexity should be justified by actual retention needs.

The compiler checks const access and pointer types; it cannot prove that the key includes every meaningful field. At runtime, map lookup compares keys and finds a matching entry. std::map lookup takes logarithmic comparisons in the number of styles. shared_ptr adds a control block and ownership bookkeeping. Neither cost disappears because the design has a name.

slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch11.json → Calculate the tradeoff before calling it an optimization
slides.title: Calculate the tradeoff before calling it an optimization
keyPoints: Suppose N marks each have U bytes of unique state and would otherwise carry S bytes of shared payload.
This example does not report exact saved bytes because object layout, string storage, allocator overhead, and platform details matter.
slides.narration:
Suppose N marks each have U bytes of unique state and would otherwise carry S bytes of shared payload. The direct representation costs roughly N times (U + S), ignoring container and allocation overhead. With K distinct styles and a per-mark handle of H bytes, sharing costs roughly N times (U + H) plus K times S, plus pool and control-block overhead. When K is nearly N or S is tiny, sharing may lose. When S is large and K is much smaller than N, it can win substantially.

This example does not report exact saved bytes because object layout, string storage, allocator overhead, and platform details matter. Measure the real workload. Also test semantic isolation: changing a mark's position must not change another mark, and equal style keys should share exactly when that is part of the pool contract. Flyweight is a targeted optimization, not a reason to turn every small value into a shared pointer.

question.prompt: What should a memory test measure besides pool.count()?
question.answer: Count retained styles and client references over time. A small current pool does not imply little live memory if old marks keep earlier styles alive.

slides.title: Read const on the object, not just the handle
keyPoints: shared_ptr<const Style> gives read-only shared state
const shared_ptr<Style> only fixes one handle
The chapter creates an actually const Style
slides.narration: A shared pointer is an owning handle: several handles can keep the same object alive. In shared_ptr<const Style>, const describes the Style reached through the handle, so field updates through that handle are forbidden. Putting const before shared_ptr instead fixes that particular handle variable; it can still reach a mutable Style. This distinction matters because one change to shared mutable style would appear in all marks using it. The chapter calls make_shared<const Style>, making the allocated object itself const, rather than retaining a secret mutable owner elsewhere. Each style is fully initialized and then read. Changing style means choosing another style owner, not quietly editing the shared object.
actions: Point to both const placements and ask what each prevents.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch11.json → Read the shared pointer type carefully

question.prompt: Does const shared_ptr<Style> prevent pointer->size = 20?
question.answer: No. The handle itself cannot be reseated, but the pointed-to Style remains mutable.

slides.title: A copy of an owner is not a copy of the style
keyPoints: Copies share ownership of one Style
Map entries and Marks both keep it alive
Last-owner destruction ends the Style lifetime
slides.narration: Follow owners rather than guessing from variable names. StylePool's map owns one handle for each retained style. A successful get returns another handle to the same object. Copying that handle updates ownership bookkeeping; it does not copy the style payload. Each Mark then owns a handle, so destroying the pool does not necessarily destroy a style. The style remains alive until its final strong owner disappears. The current sharing graph has no back pointer from Style to the pool or to marks, so it does not create an ownership cycle. In a review, label these links as shared ownership. An arrow that suggests one mark exclusively owns the style would teach the wrong lifetime.
actions: Count the owners after a map entry, two local handles, and two Marks refer to one style.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch11.json → Read the shared pointer type carefully

question.prompt: Why can survivor safely read a style after a short-lived pool is destroyed?
question.answer: survivor still owns a shared_ptr, so destroying the pool releases only the pool’s owner, not the final owner.

slides.title: Identity and equality answer different questions
keyPoints: Equal complete keys reuse one retained object
Different keys request different styles
Clearing the pool ends its identity promise for later lookups
slides.narration: Two styles can have equal field values without being the same object. Pointer equality checks object identity in this example. Before clearing the pool, repeated requests for the same key return the same retained object. The solution lab then clears the map. Old marks remain valid because their owners keep the old object alive, but a later lookup must create a new object for that key. Its name and size equal the earlier values, while its pointer differs because the old object still exists. This is not a contradiction. The pool guarantees reuse among its currently retained entries. Decide whether callers need equal appearance or stable identity across a reset before writing a stronger promise.
actions: Compare the solution’s replacement != first test with its equal name and size tests.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch11.json → Trace a lookup and a draw

question.prompt: After clear, should pointer inequality imply a different visible drawing style?
question.answer: No. The new object may have equal style values even though it has a distinct identity.

slides.title: Moving a Mark still copies in this chapter
keyPoints: Mark explicitly declares copy operations
No implicit move constructor is generated
std::move changes the expression category; it does not itself transfer anything
slides.narration: The chapter includes a subtle lifetime choice. Mark explicitly defaults its copy constructor and copy assignment. That choice suppresses automatic generation of a move constructor. When the example constructs copied from std::move(left), the available copy constructor can accept the argument and copies its shared owner. Both marks remain usable. The name std::move is easy to overread: it permits move-aware overload selection, but it does not itself remove an object from storage or force a move operation to exist. Here the value-like copy policy avoids leaving a moved-from Mark with a null style that draw would dereference. If you later add moving, define and test the moved-from contract.
actions: Ask learners to predict whether left.draw remains valid after the chapter’s std::move expression.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch11.json → Trace a lookup and a draw

question.prompt: Why does std::move(left) not prove that left lost its style owner?
question.answer: It is a cast-like expression; overload resolution chooses the available copy constructor because Mark has no generated move constructor.

slides.title: A sharing budget must include the handles
keyPoints: Direct estimate: N × (U + S)
Shared estimate: N × (U + H) + K × S + overhead
Savings require enough repeated payload
slides.narration: Let N be the number of marks. Let U be bytes unique to each mark, S the shared payload size, K the number of distinct styles, and H the per-mark handle size. The direct design roughly uses N times U plus S. Sharing roughly uses N times U plus H, then adds K copies of S and the pool's own overhead. These are estimates, not exact sizeof promises. For example, with ten thousand marks, one thousand payload bytes per style, and only ten styles, the repeated payload shrinks greatly. If nearly every mark has a unique style or the payload is tiny, lookup and handle costs may outweigh the saving. Measure the actual workload.
actions: Use N=10000, S=1000, K=10 to compare payload copies before discussing overhead.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch11.json → Calculate the tradeoff before calling it an optimization

question.prompt: Which workload makes sharing less attractive even when the code works correctly?
question.answer: K close to N or a tiny S leaves little repeated payload to remove while retaining pool and handle costs.

keyPoints: Read the ownership relationships in the named example.
One active pool returns the same object for the same key.
Published Style objects are immutable.
slides.narration:
Each hollow-diamond link is explicitly labeled shared owner, rather than exclusive composition. Both marks reach the same immutable Style but keep separate x members. The pool keeps another strong owner. A reference count tracks these owners; the Style is destroyed only after the last strong owner releases it. The diagram uses shared aggregation to show the non-exclusive relationship; the C++ shared_ptr contract supplies the precise lifetime rule.

A map interns immutable Style objects by a complete structured key. shared_ptr allows marks to retain styles after a pool is destroyed.

Share measured heavy immutable data. Keep the key, lifetime policy, and per-use state obvious so later fields do not accidentally change sharing semantics.

question.prompt: Why is this solution a reasonable extension, and could another design work?
question.answer: The solution clears the map. Existing shared_ptr owners keep old styles alive. The next request creates a new equal-valued object because the old entry is absent. This is a deliberate pool-lifetime identity rule: sharing is guaranteed among active entries, not across every clearing operation for the entire process.

question.prompt: Explain Flyweight without reciting its class names.
question.answer: A map interns immutable Style objects by a complete structured key. shared_ptr allows marks to retain styles after a pool is destroyed. Store style fields by value for a small number of small styles. Integer style IDs into a stable central table can use less per-mark memory but require a clear table lifetime and ID-validity contract.

slides.title: Retention is a policy; it is not automatically a leak
keyPoints: Strong map owners retain unused styles
clear releases pool ownership only
Weak entries need expiry handling
slides.narration: A memory graph can be correct and still retain more data than the application wants. Our map holds strong owners until entries are cleared or the pool dies. If all marks using one style disappear, the map can still keep that style alive for reuse. Calling that a missing-delete leak would misdiagnose the code. The question is whether the retention policy fits the workload. A bounded cache, explicit clear, or weak entries may be appropriate in a long-running editor. A weak pointer does not keep the style alive, so lookup must detect an expired object and recreate it. That adds states and tests. Do not add this complexity merely because weak ownership sounds cheaper.
actions: Ask learners to distinguish an unreachable leaked object from an intentionally retained map entry.

question.prompt: Does clear make existing Marks invalid?
question.answer: No. Their shared owners keep styles alive; clear removes only the pool’s owners and entries.

slides.title: Diagnose the symptom before replacing the mechanism
keyPoints: Wrong size: inspect key completeness
All marks change: inspect shared mutability
Growing cache: inspect retention policy
slides.narration: Three failures look like a sharing problem but have different causes. A request for size twenty that draws size twelve suggests an incomplete key. Editing one style and changing many marks suggests unintended shared mutation. Memory growth after deleting drawings suggests a retention policy that needs a limit. None is fixed by blindly replacing one smart pointer type with another. Also check the local invariant that every Mark has a nonnull style owner before draw uses it. The constructor rejects a missing owner for that reason. Tests should cover equal keys, different keys, rejected input, independent positions, and survival beyond the pool's scope. Together they describe what sharing actually promises.
actions: Give learners one symptom and require both a likely source location and a regression test.

question.prompt: Which test distinguishes per-use position from shared style?
question.answer: Create two Marks with the same Style owner and different x values; their drawings must retain those different positions.

slides.title: Explain the optimization without hiding the cost
keyPoints: Intent: reduce repeated state
Mechanism: complete-key reuse of immutable objects
Boundary: independent per-use values and explicit retention
slides.narration: A useful explanation of Flyweight begins with repeated data, not with shared_ptr. We measured that many uses carry the same large stable payload. We split that payload from per-use values, stored it once per complete key, and gave each use an owner that preserves its lifetime. Immutability prevents one use from changing every other use. The price is lookup, handles, bookkeeping, and a retention policy. If the direct representation is already small and clear, keeping it may be the better engineering decision. For a new drawing feature such as color, first ask whether color belongs to shared style or individual use. The answer controls the key, storage, and tests.
actions: Ask for a design review explanation that includes both a benefit and a measured cost.

question.prompt: When should color enter the pool key?
question.answer: When color is part of the shared style whose identity determines interchangeability; per-use color would instead stay outside the shared object.
